Chapter Three: The Excursion Thereupon the King said to the Crown Prince:
"You should go on an excursion."
The Prince thought to himself, "Having long remained within the deep palace, I have desired to go out on an excursion; now I shall surely obtain my wish.

The King issued a decree throughout the kingdom that the Prince was about to depart, ordering that the streets and alleys be strictly tidied, sprinkled with water, swept clean, and perfumed with incense; silk banners and canopies were to be suspended, ensuring everything was fresh and immaculate.

The Crown Prince was escorted by a procession of a thousand chariots and ten thousand horsemen as he first emerged from the eastern city gate. At that time, there was a deity of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven named Nandīghoṣa, who, wishing for the Crown Prince to renounce the world with speed to rescue and deliver the ten directions from the blazing fires of the three poisons, vowed to rain down the water of the Dharma to extinguish those poisonous flames.

Nandīpāla transformed himself into an old man sitting by the roadside; his hair was white and his teeth had fallen out; his skin was slack and his face was wrinkled; his flesh had wasted away and his spine was hunched; his limbs were withered and bent; tears and mucus flowed from his eyes and nose; saliva dripped continuously; he gasped for breath with upturned shoulders; his complexion was dark and sallow; warts grew on his head and hands; his body trembled with fear; and foul secretions issued from him as he sat upon them.
The Crown Prince asked,
"Who is this? The divine being awakened the servant, and the servant said:
“An old man. “What constitutes being old?
He replied:

"Now, as for 'the aged': their years are advanced and their faculties have matured; their physical form changes and their complexion declines; their vital energy is faint and their strength exhausted; food does not digest; their bones and joints seem ready to fall apart; they require assistance to sit or rise; their eyesight dims and their hearing becomes deaf; they forget immediately what they have said; their speech is constantly tinged with sorrow; their remaining life is but brief—therefore, they are called 'the aged.'"
The Prince sighed and said:
"In the world, human life is subject to this affliction of old age; for the foolish who crave and love it, what is there to enjoy?
All things born in spring wither and die in autumn and winter; old age arrives as swiftly as a flash of lightning—how can this body be relied upon?"
Then he spoke in verse:
"With old age, the complexion fades; With illness, one loses luster.
The skin sags and the muscles shrink; The approach of death draws near."
In old age, the form undergoes transformation, comparable to an ancient chariot;
the Dharma can eliminate suffering, so one should study it with diligence.
Life is wasting away day and night; one should exert effort while there is still time.
The truths of the world are impermanent; do not be deluded and fall into darkness.
You should learn to light the lamp of the mind, training yourself to seek wisdom.
Free from defilement and untainted by impurity, hold the torch and observe the stages of the Path.
Thereupon, the Prince immediately turned his chariot back; pitying all beings who suffer such great afflictions, he was filled with sorrow and found no joy.
The King asked his attendant:
"The Prince went out for a stroll; for what reason did he return so quickly?"
The servant replied, "On the road I encountered an old man, which caused me deep sorrow and unhappiness.
Returning to the palace, he was filled with melancholy thoughts; after several years his condition slightly improved, and he wished once again to go out on an excursion.
The King issued an edict throughout the kingdom that the Crown Prince was about to depart; he forbade all foul odors and impurities, commanding that none should remain by the roadside.
Thereupon, the Crown Prince mounted his carriage and went out through the southern gate of the city.

The deity transformed himself into a sick man by the side of the road; his body was emaciated yet his belly was distended, his frame was jaundiced and withered, and he coughed and vomited. His hundred joints were racked with agonizing pain, and his nine apertures were leaking and ruined. Impurities submerged him from within; his eyes could not see forms and his ears could not hear sounds. He groaned and gasped for breath, groping at empty space with his hands and feet, crying out for his parents and piteously longing for his wife and children.
The Crown Prince asked,
"What is this? His servant replied:
"You are ill. "In what way are you ill?
He replied:

"Human beings have four great elements: earth, water, fire, and wind. There are one hundred and one major ailments, which, through their mutual friction, result in four hundred and four diseases occurring simultaneously. Such a person will inevitably suffer from extreme cold, extreme heat, extreme hunger, extreme satiety, excessive drinking, or extreme thirst; because they lose the proper measure of moderation and their patterns of sleeping and rising become irregular, these illnesses are brought about."
The Prince sighed and said:

"I dwell in wealth and honor, possessing all that the world prizes; my food and drink delight my palate, and I have let my mind run wild in self-indulgence, indulging in the five desires without being able to awaken to it myself. I too shall surely fall ill—how am I any different from him?"
He then spoke in verse:
"How fragile is this body! It is always composed of the four great elements;
From its nine orifices flow impurities, And it is subject to old age and illness."
"Birth in the heavens is entirely impermanent; among humans there is the sorrow of old age and illness.
Contemplating the body as a bubble in the rain, what in this world can be a source of joy?
Thereupon, the Prince turned his chariot back toward the palace, reflecting that all beings are subject to these great afflictions.
The king asked his attendant:
"The prince went out on an excursion; how was it this time?
The attendant replied:
"Whenever he encountered a sick person, he became unhappy.
After several years, his condition slightly improved, and he wished to go out on an excursion again.
The King issued a decree throughout the kingdom: "The Crown Prince is about to go out; therefore, cleanse all foul places so that they do not lie near the roads."

As he exited through the western city gate, the heavens manifested a dead man being carried out of the city on a litter. His family followed the carriage, wailing and crying out to heaven: "How can you abandon us? We shall be parted forever!"
The Crown Prince asked,
"What is this? The servant replied:
"A dead person.
"What constitutes being dead?
He replied:
"Death is the ultimate end; the spirit has departed.

The four great elements seek to disperse, and the soul-spirit finds no rest. Wind departs and breath ceases; fire is extinguished and the body grows cold. Wind comes first, followed by fire, and then the soul-spirit departs."

The body remained upright, devoid of further sensation; within ten days, the flesh decayed and blood flowed, becoming bloated, putrid, and foul-smelling, such that not a single part was fit to be taken.

Within the body there are worms that turn back to devour it; the sinews and veins rot away, the bones and joints fall apart, and the skull lies in one place. The spine, ribs, shoulders, arms, thighs, shins, and toes each lie in a different spot, while birds and beasts vie with one another to come and eat them.
"Devas, nāgas, spirits, kings, and commoners—whether poor or wealthy, noble or humble—none are exempt from this affliction.
The Prince sighed deeply and spoke in verse:
"Beholding old age, sickness, and death, The Prince’s heart let out a long sigh."
Human life is impermanent; my own body is likewise so.
This body is but a thing destined for death, while the spirit follows formless laws.
Even if one were to die and be born again, the consequences of one's sins and blessings would not perish.
From beginning to end, this is not for but a single lifetime;
following from ignorance and craving for a long duration, one undergoes suffering and pleasure from this point on. When the body dies, the spirit does not perish.
Neither in the sky nor in the midst of the ocean, nor by entering into mountain clefts or between rocks—[can one escape].
"There is no place on earth where one can dwell in safety and escape death.

Thereupon, the Prince turned his chariot and returned to the palace; out of compassion for sentient beings who suffer the great afflictions of old age, sickness, and death, he was filled with sorrow and ceased to eat.
The king asked his attendant,
"When the prince went out on an excursion, was there any pleasure for him?
The attendant immediately replied to the king:
"Having encountered a dead person, I have consequently fallen into a state of unhappiness.
After several years, his condition slightly improved, and wishing again to travel and sightsee, he prepared his carriage and went out through the northern city gate.
The deity again transformed himself into a śramaṇa, wearing dharma robes and holding an alms bowl, walking with composed and dignified steps, his eyes never leaving the path ahead.
The Crown Prince asked,
"Who is this person?
His servant replied:
“A śramaṇa! [The king asked,] “What constitutes a śramaṇa?

[The Buddha replied,] “I have heard that the Way of the śramaṇa consists in abandoning home, wife, and children; casting off love and desire; severing the six sense-faculties; maintaining the precepts and non-action; and attaining single-mindedness. When one attains single-mindedness, then all myriad evils are extinguished.”
The Way of single-mindedness is called Arhat; an Arhat is a true person.

Sounds and forms cannot defile them, honors and positions cannot humble them; they are as immovable as the earth, having already escaped sorrow and suffering, and are sovereign over both life and death.
The Prince said: "Excellent!
Only this is truly refreshing."
He then spoke in verse: “Alas!
There is this suffering: The afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death;
The spirit returns to enter into transgression, Passing through all manner of toil and hardship.”
"Now I shall extinguish all sufferings; birth, old age, sickness, and death shall be eliminated.
I shall no longer meet with craving, and I will forever attain nirvāṇa.
Thereupon, the Prince immediately turned his chariot back and returned, observing a fast and contemplating in silence.
The king asked his attendant:
"The prince has gone out again; does he perhaps find pleasure there?
The attendant replied:
"Having seen the śramaṇa, he has become even more distressed and refuses food and drink.

Upon hearing this, the king was greatly incensed; raising his hand, he struck himself, saying, "I previously commanded him to cultivate the Way, yet now the Prince has suddenly encountered such an inauspicious sight. His crime deserves execution."
He immediately summoned his ministers and ordered each to propose a plan or devise a stratagem by which the Crown Prince might be prevented from leaving home to practice the Way.
One minister said:
"The Crown Prince should be appointed to oversee agricultural cultivation; by taxing his mental faculties with such labor, he will be made to cease thinking of the Way."
He then provided a thousand sets of farming implements and oxen, and led his male and female servants, both great and small, to the fields to supervise their labor.

The Prince sat beneath a Jambu tree and saw the plowmen tilling the soil, which brought forth insects; furthermore, he saw that heaven had transformed the oxen's necks to become broken and collapsed, causing the insects to fall down in a stream, while crows followed and pecked them to swallow.

Again, he became a frog and pursued a cricket to eat it; a snake emerged from its burrow and swallowed the frog; a peacock flew down and pecked and swallowed the snake; an eagle swooped down and seized the peacock; then a vulture came and pounced upon and devoured the eagle.
Seeing these classes of sentient beings preying upon one another, the Bodhisattva was moved by compassion and attained the first dhyāna beneath a tree.
As the sun’s rays blazed intensely, the tree bent its branches so that they shaded his body.
The King, constantly thinking of the Crown Prince and noting that he had never experienced hardship while remaining within the palace, asked his attendants:
"How is the Crown Prince?
They replied:
"He is now beneath a Jambu tree, practicing one-pointed meditative concentration.
The king said, "I ordered the overseers of the construction to disturb his thoughts, yet he remains in meditative concentration; how does this differ from staying at home?"
The king issued orders to prepare his carriage and went forth to welcome him.
From afar he saw the Prince; the branches of the tree curved to provide shade, and his divine radiance was extraordinary.
Not knowing who he was, the king dismounted from his horse and prostrated himself in salutation at that moment, whereupon they returned together.
Before he had even reached the city gate, countless thousands of people came forth with flowers and incense to welcome him; all the physiognomists proclaimed his immeasurable longevity.
The King asked:
"For what reason?"
The brahmin replied,
"At dawn, when the sun rises, the seven treasures shall arrive.
The king was greatly rejoiced, certain that he would become a holy wheel-turning monarch.

Chapter Five: Leaving Home At that time, the Prince returned to the palace and reflected deeply. Mindful of the purity of the Way, he realized it was not fitting to remain at home; he should instead dwell among the mountains and forests to cultivate his essence and practice dhyāna.
When he reached the age of nineteen, on the seventh day of the fourth month, he vowed to leave the household life.
After midnight, when the morning star appeared, the various devas filled the void of space, exhorting the Prince to depart.
At that time, Gopī saw five dreams and immediately woke up in alarm. The Prince asked her, "For what reason have you awakened in such a state of alarm?
She replied:

"Just now, within my dream, I saw Mount Sumeru collapse, the bright moon fall to the ground, the luster of jewels suddenly vanish, my topknot fall to the earth, and someone snatch away my parasol; for this reason, I woke up in alarm."
The Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"These five dreams pertain only to my own person; I shall surely leave the household life.
He then said to Gopī:

"Mount Sumeru does not crumble, the bright moon continues to shine, the luster of the jewel does not fade, and the topknot has not fallen; the parasol remains here now. Rest in peace for now; do not worry about losing the parasol."
Thereupon the devas said, "The Prince must depart; we fear he will cause delay.
They summoned Aśman, known in the human realm as the deity of suppression, who had just entered the palace and was suppressing all within the kingdom into sleep.

At that time, Nandīpāla transformed all the palaces into burial mounds; the *kauravya* musicians and courtesans all became corpses, their bones and joints scattered and their skulls lying in different places, bloated, putrid, and foul-smelling, with dark bruises and pus and blood flowing and spreading in continuous succession.
The Prince surveyed the palace buildings and saw them all as nothing but tombs; owls, foxes, jackals, wolves, birds, and beasts flew and ran about among them.
Observing that all things possessed were like illusions, like transformations, like dreams, and like echoes—all ultimately returning to emptiness—yet the foolish cling to them.
He immediately called for Chandaka and urgently ordered him to saddle the horse.
Chandaka said, "The sky has not yet dawned; where would you go by saddling the horse?"
The Prince spoke these verses to Chandaka:
"I have no delight in the world now; Chandaka, do not delay.
Let my original vow be fulfilled, and I shall eliminate your suffering throughout the three periods of time."
Thereupon, Chandaka immediately went to saddle the horse, but the horse began to leap and kick, refusing to allow him to approach.
He returned and reported to the Prince:
"The horse cannot be saddled at this time."
The Bodhisattva went himself and patted the horse’s back, speaking these verses:
"Long have I dwelt within birth and death; From this day forth, riding shall cease.
Kanthaka, you have escorted me out; When I attain the Way, I shall not forget you."
When the horse had been saddled,
Bāṣpa thought to himself:
"Now I shall set foot upon the ground and move the hearts of people both within and without."
The Four Divine Beings received him as he lifted his foot, ensuring that his feet did not touch the ground.
When the horse then wished to neigh, they caused its sound to be heard far and near;
the celestial deities dispersed the horse's voice, causing it all to enter into empty space.
The Prince immediately mounted his horse and set out toward the city gate; the devas, nāgas, spirits, Śakra, Brahmā, and the four heavenly kings all escorted and followed him, filling the void above.
At that time, a deity of the city gate manifested in human form and, bowing his head, said:
"The kingdom of Kapilavastu is the very center of the world.
It is prosperous, joyful, and its people are at peace; for what reason do you abandon it and depart?"
The Prince answered in verse:
"Birth and death have lasted for a long time, And the spirit has traversed the five realms.
Once my original vow is fulfilled, I shall open the gate to Nirvana."
Thereupon, the city gates opened spontaneously, and he departed through them, flying away.
At dawn, having traveled four hundred and eighty *li*, he arrived at the country of Aṇumā, which in the Han language is called "Ever-Full."
The Prince dismounted from his horse, removed the precious robes, necklaces, and jeweled crown from his body, and gave them all to Chandaka, saying:
"You shall take the horse back and offer my thanks to the Great King and the ministers of the realm."
Candaka said:
"I shall now follow you and provide whatever you require; I cannot return alone and let the horse go.
There are many venomous insects, tigers, wolves, and lions in the mountains—who would provide you with food, drink, water, and bedding?"
"How can I obtain it? I must follow after it, even at the cost of my own life. Kṣāntivādin knelt down on his right knee;
tears fell as he licked [the horse's] feet. Seeing water, he would not drink; finding grass, he would not eat. He cried out with flowing tears, pacing back and forth without leaving.
The Crown Prince spoke again in verse:
"The body, though strong, is crushed by disease; Vitality, though flourishing, declines with old age.
Death brings separation from those one loves— How can one find joy in this world?"
Thereupon, Chandaka wept bitterly, prostrated at his feet, and led the horse away to take his leave.

Before he had reached the capital city, forty *li* outside, the white horse neighed mournfully; its sound resounded throughout the kingdom, and everyone within the realm cried out, "The Prince is returning!"
The people of the entire kingdom came forth in a continuous stream to welcome him, yet they saw only Candra returning empty-handed, leading the horse.
Seeing this, Jyotiṣka threw himself down at the foot of the palace steps; he went forward to embrace the horse’s neck, his tears falling in profusion.
When the King saw Qiuyi weeping, his five internal organs were all shattered with grief; suppressing himself, he addressed him, saying:
"My son, you have studied the Way of Nature.
When the ministers and citizens of the kingdom saw the King and Qiuyi sobbing and weeping in sorrow, there was none among them who was not deeply moved by their distress.
While Qiuyi thought day and night about this, the King summoned his ministers and said:
"I have an only son who has abandoned me to enter the mountains.
You all must now be ranked in order; let the number reach five persons who shall follow and attend upon the Prince together, and be careful not to return midway."
"Having attained his departure from worldly life, the Prince leaped for joy and entered the city with calm and measured steps.
When the people of the kingdom beheld the Prince, they rejoiced without ever growing weary."
The Prince, having departed from affection and love, and distanced himself from the roots of all suffering and affliction, desired to shave his hair; however, being in haste, he had no implements.
Śakra held forth a blade, and the celestial deities received his hair and departed. Thereupon, he proceeded forward once more.
The people of the kingdom followed and watched him.
Thereupon he left the city, proceeded a short distance further, and arrived at the kingdom of Magadha; he entered through the right gate and exited through the left gate.

The people within the kingdom—men and women, great and small—whoever beheld the Prince, some called him a celestial being, while others called him Śakra, Brahmā, a heavenly deity, or a Nāga King; they leaped for joy, not knowing what kind of divinity he was.
The Prince, knowing their thoughts, stepped down from the road and sat beneath a tree; the people gathered around him, gazing upon him with joy.
At that time, King Bimbisāra asked his ministers and officials:
"Why is the city so silent? Why is there not a single sound?"
He replied:
"This morning, a man of the Way passed through the capital. His radiant appearance and majestic deportment were unlike anything in this world.
The people of the country, both great and small, followed him out to watch, and they have not yet returned."
Thereupon, the king and his ministers went out to visit the Daoist master.
Seeing from afar that the Prince’s radiant marks were exceptionally wondrous, he asked the Prince:
"What deity are you?"
The Prince replied,
"I am no deity! If you are not a deity, from what country have you come?"
"What is your clan?
The Prince replied, "I come from the east of Mount Gandhamādana and the north of the Snowy Mountains; my country is named Kapilavastu, my father is named Śuddhodana, and my mother is named Māyā."
Bimbisāra asked, "Could it be Siddhārtha?
He replied:
"It is so! he exclaimed, rising in alarm to prostrate at his feet:

"The Prince was born with many wonders; his physical marks are radiant and distinct. He shall rule over the four continents as a Wheel-Turning Sage King, and the people of the four seas look up in eager anticipation for the arrival of the divine treasures."
"Why have you abandoned the celestial throne to throw yourself among the mountains and thickets?
You must surely have some extraordinary insight; I wish to hear your resolve.
The Prince replied:

"According to what I have observed, among heaven, earth, people, and things, there is birth and death; there are three kinds of intense suffering—the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death—which cannot be avoided."

Being a vessel of suffering, one faces immeasurable grief and fear; yet if one is held in honor and favor, there arises arrogance and indolence, as well as a greedy pursuit of pleasure, whereby the world is afflicted by calamity. Because I loathe this, I wish to enter the mountains.
The elders said:
"Now, old age, sickness, and death are the natural constants of the world; why should you alone be so preoccupied with anxiety?
To abandon your noble title and live in seclusion and obscurity, thereby exhausting your body—is this not difficult?"
Thereupon, the Prince spoke in verse:
"If one could remain in the womb without being defiled by impurity;
if one could remain in purity without being stained by impurity;"
If suffering were not so manifold and beyond counting;
if it were otherwise—then who would not delight in the world?
If the human form did not undergo such various transformations as aging;
If one could ensure that those who practice virtue do not engage in evil deeds,
and if one could ensure that the suffering of separation from loved ones did not occur—
if this were possible, who would not delight in the world?
May it be so that when one is ill and emaciated, there shall be no further great fear;
may it be so that in future lives, there shall be no evil adversaries;
may it be so that even if one falls into hell, there shall be no suffering or pain.
Even if it were so, who would not delight in the world?
If only the forms of youth did not undergo decay;
if only one could avoid attachment to that which is undesirable.
If, when the time of death arrives, there were no manifold fears;
if it were truly so, who would not delight in the world?
If ignorance were not regarded as a profound darkness;
If one could ensure that anger does not become a powerful enemy,
and if one could ensure that the mind of the five sensual pleasures does not become defiled by evil—
were it possible to do so in this way, who would not delight in the world?
May I not dwell together with those deluded people;
may I personally distance myself from all deluded dharmas;
and may those deluded people be devoid of conceptual thought.
If it were thus, who would not delight in the world?
If all evil seeds were not of various kinds;
if all evils were completely extinguished and naturally departed from people;
If all evil thoughts were made free of conceptualization;
if it were thus, who would not delight in the world?
If the evils of the world were made supreme and most honored;
If one could cause evil conduct to be extinguished so that it does not arise again;
if one could cause all evil conduct to be exhausted and found to have no reality—
if this were possible, who would not delight in the world?
May the devas enjoy their merit and remain forever unmoved;
may the lifespan of worldly people endure eternally;
and may all places not become destinations for rebirth.
If it were thus, who would not delight in the world?
If only the various aggregates (skandhas) were not enemies,
and if only the six sense bases (āyatanas) were free from suffering and affliction!
"If it were possible to make all the worlds free from suffering,
and if such a thing were indeed so, who would not delight in the world?
"In this regard, it is as you gentlemen have said:"

"One should not worry in advance, thinking: 'When I have become king and old age arrives followed by illness, at the time when death is imminent, will there be anyone who can take this misfortune upon themselves in my stead?'"
Since there is no one who can take one’s place, how can one not worry?
In this world, there are compassionate fathers and filial sons whose love penetrates to the very marrow of their bones; yet even at the moment of death, they cannot substitute for one another.

If this false body reaches the day when suffering arrives, even if one occupies a high position with six types of relatives by one's side, it is like setting up a candle for a blind person; what benefit is there for one who has no eyes?
I observe all conditioned phenomena; they are entirely impermanent, all transformations and none are real. Pleasure is slight while suffering is abundant.
The body does not belong to oneself; the world is empty and void, difficult to inhabit for long.
All things that arise must die; all undertakings that succeed must fail; security is followed by peril; and gain is followed by loss.
The myriad phenomena are in constant turmoil, yet they must all return to emptiness. The spirit is formless; when it is restless and turbid, it lacks clarity.
The cycle of death and rebirth brings calamities that do not end with a single lifetime alone.
Yet, because they are shrouded by craving and ensnared in the net of ignorance, beings are submerged in the river of birth and death, unable to awaken.

Therefore, I wish to enter the mountains and concentrate my mind on the purity of the four *ārūpya-samāpattis*, transcending form and extinguishing ill-will, severing craving, contemplating emptiness, and remaining free from attachment or aversion. This will be to return to the source and revert to the root; only when I have emerged from its foundation and attained what I desire shall there be great peace.
King Bimbisāra and the various elders, their hearts filled with joy and their minds liberated, said:
"The Prince’s resolve is sublime and rare in this world; he will surely attain the Way of the Buddha. We pray that you will deliver us first."
The Prince remained silent and departed; then, as he proceeded, he thought to himself:
"Now that I am entering the mountains, what use have I for these precious robes?
The foolish people of the world are all endangered by wealth."
He then saw a hunter driving his game, yet wearing the dharma robes.
The Prince thought with joy:
"These are the robes of a true person, the compassionate garments for crossing over the world; why does this hunter wear them?"
"I have resolved in my mind to trade, so that my heart's desire may be fulfilled.
He then took the golden-threaded garment and traded it for the *śāṇa* cloth of the Dharma.
The hunter was inwardly filled with joy, and the Bodhisattva felt the same.
The Prince wore a saṃkakṣikā that was soft, fresh, and pure; looking upon his saṃghāṭī robe, it was indistinguishable from that of the Buddha, whereupon he entered the mountains.
When the Bodhisattva obtained the Dharma-robe, his joy was illuminated by a radiant light.

The practitioners in the mountain forests—some called Āraṇas and others Kālaṇas—who had studied for many years, were fully endowed with the four dhyānas and had attained the five supernatural powers, were struck with alarm and fear upon seeing the light, wondering: "What auspicious omen is this?"
They then went out together from their retreat and saw the Prince from afar, saying:
"This is Siddhārtha; he has now indeed gone forth into homelessness.
Welcome, Siddhārtha! Please sit upon this couch; you may now partake of these cool springs and fine fruits."
And he spoke in verse:
"When the Sun King first rises, He stands upon the mountain peak;
Therefore, with the light of wisdom, He illuminates all living beings."
"If one gazes upon their facial features, one never tires of doing so;
therefore, the Way and its Virtue are supreme, peerless and without equal.
At that time, the Bodhisattva spoke in verse:
"Though one may cultivate the four meditative concentrations, if one does not know the unsurpassed wisdom, the path of the mind takes right awakening as its foundation;
it does not consist in serving heterodox deities."
"Practicing what is conventional while calling it true, they seek the Brahma-heaven throughout the long night;
for this reason they do not recognize the Way, and thus they revolve and fall into birth and death.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness and thought universally of sentient beings—aged, decrepit, and utterly ignorant—who could not escape the pains of illness, death, and loss, and whom he desired to liberate by unifying their minds.

One gives rise to the mind of compassion, pitying all beings who suffer from hunger, thirst, cold, heat, gain, loss, transgression, and hardship, desiring to bring them peace and security and unify their minds;
one gives rise to the mind of sympathetic joy, reflecting that all in the world face the afflictions of sorrow, suffering, fear, and calamity, desiring to make them tranquil and unify their minds;

one gives rise to the mind of protection, wishing to deliver sentient beings from the five realms and eight difficulties who are deluded and obscured, failing to see the Right Path, and intending to rescue and sustain them so they may attain the Unconditioned, thereby unifying their minds.

Rejoicing not at gain and feeling no sorrow upon encountering misfortune, one abandons the eight worldly concerns—profit and loss, disrepute and fame, praise and blame, suffering and pleasure—and remains unshaken by them, thereby accomplishing the practice of the second dhyāna.

"Proceeding further, he arrived at the Sna River. The river was level and even, abounding with many fruit trees; everywhere there were flowing springs and bathing pools, which were pure and clean, free from centipedes, bees, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, and fleas."
There was a Daoist master from Chuanyang named Sina, who taught five hundred disciples and had them practice his arts.
At that time, the Bodhisattva sat beneath a śāla tree, having resolved to seek the unsurpassed, true, and correct path for the sake of all beings.
The devas offered him ambrosia, but the Bodhisattva would not accept it at all. He vowed to himself to sustain his vital energy by consuming only one sesame seed and one grain of rice per day.

For six years he sat upright; his body became so emaciated that skin and bone were joined together. His essence was profound and still, and he remained silent with a single mind. Internally, he contemplated *ānāpāna*—first counting, second following, third stopping, fourth observing, fifth returning, and sixth purifying. His will roamed through the third and fourth dhyānas and emerged from the twelve gates of liberation; his mind was never distracted. His supernormal powers were wondrously perfected as he abandoned desire and unwholesome dharmas. No longer were there the five hindrances, nor did he receive the five desires; all evils were naturally extinguished. His mindfulness and discernment were clear and distinct; he contemplated non-action (*asaṃskṛta*) with focused vision, like a strong man who has defeated his enemy. His mind was thus purified, and he accomplished the practice of the third dhyāna.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thought to himself:

"The Bodhisattva has sat beneath the tree for six full years; his body is emaciated and wasted. Now I shall cause the people of the world to offer food fit for a Wheel-Turning King, so as to replenish him from the hunger and exhaustion of those six years."

He then moved the two daughters, Sī and Na, so that in their dreams they saw the entire world become water, in which there was a single flower with the luster of the seven treasures; in an instant it withered and lost its original color.
He saw a man who sprinkled water upon it, whereupon it grew back as it was before.
Within the water, various flowers began to sprout their buds and emerged, covering the surface.
The two daughters woke from their dream, marvelling at such an unprecedented occurrence, and immediately informed their father.
Their father did not understand it, so he questioned the elders, but none of them could explain it.
The Heavenly Lord again descended and transformed himself into a brahmin to explain the dream to the woman, saying:
"That which you saw—a flower growing from the waters of the world—was when the Prince of King Śuddhodana was first born.
That he is now beneath the tree for six years, his body weak and his form emaciated, is the time when that flower has withered."
The person seen being revived by the sprinkling of water is one capable of offering food;
the small flowers and sprouts about to emerge are the beings in the cycle of birth and death within the five realms of existence.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately spoke in verse:
“For six years he did not lean or recline, Nor did he think of hunger or cold.
With diligence free from attachment, His body grew so thin that his skin clung to his bones.”
"You all should cultivate a respectful mind and make offerings to the Bodhisattva;
you shall obtain great merit in this present life and receive the fruit of retribution in future lives.
The woman said:
"What is the method for offering food? The Brahmin replied:

"One should take the milk of five hundred cows and have them drink from one another until it reaches a single cow. Then, one milks that one cow to prepare a porridge. As the milk porridge boils, it surges up to a height of seven *zhang*; it flows down on the left side and up on the right, and down on the right side and up on the left. One pours the porridge into the bowl, yet neither the cauldron nor the ladle is soiled."
The two maidens, with reverent solemnity, presented the gruel to the Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva thought to himself that he should first bathe before receiving the gruel; he then went to the side of a flowing stream to wash his body.
Having finished his bath and wishing to emerge from the water, a heavenly deity pressed down a tree branch; two maidens offered him milk gruel.
Having obtained its color and strength, his vigor was restored; he offered blessings and prayers of immeasurable merit, leading the women to take refuge in the Triple Gem.

When he had finished eating, he washed his hands and rinsed his mouth; having cleansed his bowl, he threw it back into the water. Before it had traveled seven *li* against the current, a celestial being transformed into a garuḍa and flew down to seize the bowl and carry it away. Taking both the bowl and the hair together, they made offerings to them and erected a stupa.
He then proceeded forward, intending to cross the Nairañjanā River.
At that time, the Bodhisattva spoke these verses:
"Crossing the waters of the Nairañjanā, Out of compassion for all people,"
The defilements of the five paths and the three poisons Are made to vanish like water purified.
When the Bodhisattva gives rise to this thought: "All beings, deluded, fall into darkness;
I shall uphold the water of the Eightfold Straight Path To wash away the stains of the three poisons."
"At that time, as he first stepped onto the shore, five hundred blue jays flew down and circled the Bodhisattva;
after circling him three times, they departed with mournful cries.
Thereupon, proceeding further, as he was about to pass by the pool of the blind dragon, the dragon was filled with great joy; leaping forth, it beheld the Bodhisattva and spoke this verse:
"How excellent it is to see Siddhārtha! Why did you come so late to save us?
Originally, you invited all the multitudes to partake of the unsurpassed nectar of immortality."
As he walks, the earth trembles, and various musical instruments sound spontaneously;
he is equal to the Buddhas of the past, and of this I have no doubt.
Now, upholding supreme wisdom, he subdues all demonic adversaries.
"Now the Buddha-sun shall shine, awakening the slumbering multitudes of living beings.

Thereupon he proceeded further and beheld from afar a grove of trees and mountains; the ground was level and even, pure and serene in every direction. The growing grass was soft and supple, sweet springs flowed in abundance, and the flowers were lush and pristine. In the midst stood a single tree, noble and extraordinary: its branches joined one after another and its leaves overlapped in succession. The colors of the flowers were dense and vibrant, like celestial adornments; a heavenly banner rested atop the tree’s summit—a sign of supreme auspiciousness, the king among all the trees in the forest.
Thereupon, he proceeded a short distance and saw a grass-cutter. The Bodhisattva then asked him:
"What is your name now? [The man replied:
"My name is Śrī, and I am now cutting śrī-grass."
"Now that you have given me this grass, all ten directions shall be auspicious.
Then Renjixiang (Auspicious Human) spoke these verses:
"Having renounced the rank of a noble king, The seven treasures, and a jade-like consort,"
Why do you now use straw for bedding, instead of couches of gold and silver,
woolen rugs and brocade cushions, and the auspicious sounds of joy and sorrow—
the true melodies of the eight classes of beings that surpass even those of the Brahma heavens?
The Bodhisattva replied in verse:
“I have made vows for incalculable eons, Desiring to deliver those on the five paths.
Now I go to fulfill my original vow; For this reason, I wish to obtain grass.”
"A man gave me a handful of tangled grass, and I took it toward the King of Trees [the Bodhi tree], thinking:
'The minds of those in the world are all in disorder; I shall set their wills aright.'"
"Taking the grass, he sprinkled it upon the ground;
exactly as he had spoken, the Bodhisattva sat upon it, and all received his grace.
The Bodhisattva established three essential points:"
"Seated upon my heart and beneath this tree, if I do not attain the Way, I shall never depart from these three vows.
Even if my flesh and bones wither away, I will remain unmoving until I have surely accomplished it.
When I surpass all Buddhas and attain the Way, may they all emerge from this single mind."

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva sat upright and entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*). He abandoned both suffering and pleasure, as well as the perceptions of sorrow and joy; his mind neither relied upon the wholesome nor adhered to the unwholesome, remaining exactly in the middle. Like a person who has bathed until clean and is covered with a white cloth—pure within and without, free from defilement on the surface or inside—the movement of his breath ceased of its own accord; in profound stillness and without change, he accomplished the practice of the fourth dhyāna.

Having attained concentration of mind, he does not abandon great compassion; through wisdom and skillful means, he thoroughly masters the essential subtleties and penetrates the practice of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
What are these thirty-seven factors?

First are the four foundations of mindfulness; second are the four right efforts; third are the four bases of power; fourth are the five faculties; fifth are the five powers; sixth are the seven factors of enlightenment; and seventh are the eightfold noble path.
Cycling through and beginning again, suffering, emptiness, and impermanence are without thought or aspiration.

"I contemplate the world: through greed, craving, and sensual desire, beings fall into the suffering of birth and death; few are able to awaken to the fact that this fundamentally arises from the twelve links of dependent origination."

What are the twelve bases? From the activity of ignorance, consciousness arises; conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form arises; from the activity of name-and-form, the six sense bases arise; conditioned by the six sense bases, contact arises; conditioned by contact, sensation arises; conditioned by sensation, craving arises; conditioned by craving, grasping arises; conditioned by grasping, existence arises; conditioned by existence, birth arises; conditioned by birth, there arise old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair—the great affliction of the mind. Thus, possessing a conscious spirit, one revolves and falls into the cycle of birth and death.

Those who wish to attain the Way should sever craving and eliminate sensual desire; being unconditioned and non-arising, ignorance (*moha*) is extinguished. When ignorance is extinguished, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are extinguished;

when volitional formations are extinguished, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is extinguished; when consciousness is extinguished, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is extinguished; when name-and-form is extinguished, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are extinguished; when the six sense bases are extinguished, contact (*sparśa*) is extinguished; when contact is extinguished, feeling (*vedanā*) is extinguished; when feeling is extinguished, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is extinguished; when craving is extinguished, grasping (*upādāna*) is extinguished; when grasping is extinguished, becoming (*bhava*) is extinguished; when becoming is extinguished, birth (*jāti*) is extinguished; and when birth is extinguished, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair—all these great afflictions—are utterly exhausted. This is called attaining the Way.
The Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"Now I shall subdue the retinue of Māra.
He immediately emitted the light from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which shook the palace of Māra.

Māra was greatly terrified and his heart was ill at ease; seeing the Bodhisattva already beneath the tree, pure and free from desire, meditating with unwearied diligence, Māra felt a poisonous agitation in his heart. His food no longer tasted sweet and he could not bear the sounds of music. He thought: "If this man achieves the Way, he will surely defeat me utterly. Before he has yet become a Buddha, I must destroy his resolve for enlightenment."
The son of Māra, Sumati—which in the Han language means "Worthy Intent"—came forward and admonished his father, saying:

"The Bodhisattva’s conduct is pure and peerless within the three realms. Having attained spontaneous supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), hundreds of millions of Brahmās and devas all go to pay him homage and serve him. This is not something that can be thwarted or destroyed by gods or men; do not engage in evil deeds and thereby ruin your own merit."
The Demon King would not listen; instead, his three daughters took charge themselves. One was named En’ài (Affection), the second Chánglè (Eternal Joy), and the third Dàlè (Great Joy).
They said, "Father King, do not worry. We shall go ourselves to destroy the Bodhisattva’s resolve for the Way. There is no need to trouble the Father King; do not worry any longer."

Thereupon, the three daughters, adorned in celestial raiment, accompanied by five hundred jade maidens, went to where the Bodhisattva was; they played the lute and sang songs of lewd desire, seeking to disturb his resolve for the Way.
The three daughters spoke again:
"Your benevolence and virtue are most profound, and you are revered by all the devas; it is fitting that there should be offerings made to you, which is why the heavens have presented us to you.
We are pure and refined, and we are in the prime of our youth; we pray that we may rise at dawn and retire at night to serve you by your side."
The Bodhisattva replied:

"You possess merit from past lives and have thus obtained this celestial body; yet you do not contemplate impermanence, but instead practice seductive charms. Though your physical form is beautiful, your heart is not upright."
It is like a painted vase filled with foul poison, which one carries about only to bring about one's own ruin.

What is so extraordinary about this? Merit cannot endure for long; through lustful evil and unwholesome conduct, one destroys one’s very foundation. When merit is exhausted and sin arrives, one falls into the three evil realms and takes the form of a beast among the six classes of beings; to escape from there is exceedingly difficult.
"You all have disturbed the human aspiration for the Way and fail to reckon with impermanence; thus you have passed through kalpas, transmigrating through the five realms of existence.
Even now, you and your kind have not yet escaped from toil and suffering."

"While I am in this world, wherever I am born, I regard those who are old as my mother, those of middle age as my elder sisters, and those who are young as my younger sisters. O sisters, each of you return to your palaces and do not commit such deeds again."

At the Bodhisattva’s single word, the three women immediately became old mothers: their hair turned white, their teeth fell out, their eyes grew dim, and their spines bent; leaning upon staffs for support, they returned home.

When Māra saw that his three daughters had all become old mothers, he became even more enraged and summoned eighteen billion ghost kings from the heavens. They surrounded the Bodhisattva for thirty-six *yojanas*, transforming themselves into innumerable forms of lions, bears, brown bears, rhinoceroses, tigers, elephants, dragons, oxen, horses, dogs, pigs, monkeys, and apes.

They have the heads of insects and the bodies of humans, with the forms of lizards and snakes and the heads of soft-shelled turtles and tortoises; they possess six eyes, or a single neck with many heads, and have teeth, tusks, claws, and talons. They shoulder mountains and vomit fire, with thunder and lightning swirling about them as they grasp halberds and spears.

The Bodhisattva’s mind was filled with compassion; he was neither startled nor terrified, not even a single hair on his body moved. His countenance became even more radiant and beautiful, and the ghost-soldiers were unable to approach him.

Then the Māra came forward and spoke a verse, asking: “The Bhikṣu, what do you seek that you sit beneath the tree, Delighting amidst the thickets and forests where venomous beasts dwell? The Bodhisattva, whose mind was imbued with compassion, answered every question asked: [He said:
“O Bhikṣu, what do you seek that you sit beneath the tree, Delighting amidst the thickets and forests where venomous beasts dwell?”
Clouds arise, fearsome and profound in their gloom; though surrounded by celestial Māras, he is not startled.
"In antiquity there was the True Path practiced by the Buddhas: serenity is supreme, for it removes all inauspiciousness.
Having perfected the most excellent Dharma that fills the treasury, I seek this seat to decisively defeat the King of Māra."
"You shall become a king who turns the golden wheel, with the seven treasures coming of their own accord to govern the four quarters;
the five sensual pleasures you enjoy shall be peerless, yet in this place there is no path for you to enter the palace."
"I have beheld the intensity of desire as like swallowing molten copper; I cast away my kingdom like spittle, having no craving for it.
Even attaining kingship brings the anxieties of old age and death; depart from this profitless talk and do not speak thus in vain."
"Why do you sit so peacefully in the forest as if speaking grand words, having abandoned your kingdom, wealth, and status to dwell in empty seclusion?
Do you not see me mobilizing the fourfold army—eighteen billion elephants, horses, and infantry?"
"I have already seen the faces of monkeys, apes, and lions;
tigers, rhinoceroses, venomous snakes, boars, and demons—all brandishing swords and blades, grasping halberds and spears, leaping and roaring, filling the air."
Even if you were to assemble a hundred million trillion divine armies, and if Māras like yourself were to come here together,
with arrows, blades, and fire-attacks falling like wind and rain— I shall not rise until I have first attained Buddhahood.
"Māra has a fundamental vow to cause me to retreat, yet I too have sworn that I shall not return empty-handed;
now, as for this field of merit of yours, how does it compare to that of the Buddha?
From this, it shall be known who attains victory."
"I once practiced joyful giving throughout my entire life, And thus presided over the Six Heavens as a Mara King.
Bhikṣus know my past meritorious deeds; Who can testify to my own claim of being immeasurable?"
"In the past, through my vows, I followed Dīpaṃkara; having received his consecration as the Buddha Śākyamuni, I sit here because anger and fearful thoughts have been exhausted;
with my mind fixed in concentration, I shall surely liberate myself and destroy your army."
The Buddhas whom I have served have been many; I have constantly bestowed wealth, treasures, food, and clothing upon others.
My benevolence, precepts, and accumulated merit are as vast as the earth; therefore, I am liberated from conceptualization and free from all suffering and hardship.
"The Bodhisattva, by the power of his wisdom, extended his hand and pressed the earth, saying, 'Let it bear witness to me.
At that moment, the entire earth shook violently, and Māra and his retinue were cast down in confusion."
The Māra king was defeated and despondent at his failure; bewildered, he retreated and squatted down, drawing lines on the ground before him.
His son further enlightened his mind, whereupon he awoke and immediately returned to the Buddha to repent his transgressions:
"I shall no longer employ weapons; with equal practice of a compassionate heart, I shall repel the demonic foes."
The world employs weapons to move the hearts of men, while I employ you sentient beings.
Even if elephants and horses have been tamed, their former habits will surely arise again;
but if one attains the ultimate taming of the Buddha-nature, once tamed by the Buddha, there is nothing that is not benevolent.
"The Lord of Heaven beholds the Buddha subduing the hosts of Māra; through patience and discipline, he tames them so that even the thoughtless enemies surrender of their own accord.
All the devas rejoice as they arrive offering flowers, exclaiming:
'The King of Unrighteousness is defeated, and the King of Dharma has triumphed!'"
Fundamentally arising from the power of equanimity and wisdom, Wisdom can immediately avert all inauspiciousness;
It can cause even enemies to become disciples— One should pay homage to the realization of the Four Immeasurables.
His face is like the full moon, his demeanor composed; His fame resounds throughout the ten directions, his virtue is like a mountain.
The features of the Buddha’s image are difficult to find a match for; One should prostrate before this immortal who delivers the world.

“Through the pure practices accumulated by the Bodhisattva over many kalpas, he reached the great compassion of the Confucian sages; his Way was naturally settled, and through the power of patience, he subdued the Māras. When the demonic armies retreated and dispersed, his concentrated mind remained as it was before. Without relying on intellectual deliberation, he was free from thoughts of sorrow or joy. That night, after midnight, he attained the three *ṛddhipādas* (the bases of supernormal power)—*ṛddhipāda* being translated in the Han language as ‘the three divine powers fully perfected’—whereby his outflows were exhausted and his fetters untied. He knew of himself the practices he had long cultivated in the past: the four bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*), namely, the concentration of diligence, the concentration of desire, the concentration of intention, and the concentration of precepts.

Having attained the dharma of transformation, whatever he desired was accomplished according to his will without further thought; his body could fly, and he could divide his single body into a hundred, a thousand, up to hundreds of millions or countless forms, and then merge them back into one.”
They can penetrate the earth, passing through stone walls as if they were nothing; they appear from one direction and then submerge or emerge from below, like waves upon water;
they can emit water and fire from their bodies;
and they can walk upon water or travel through the air without their bodies sinking or falling.
He sits and lies in mid-air like a soaring bird;
standing, he can reach the heavens and touch the sun and moon with his hand. If he wishes, he can stand upright and reach as far as the Brahma-heaven of sovereign mastery.

His eyes see through all things, his ears hear clearly, and his mind possesses foreknowledge; regarding all classes of beings—gods, humans, nāgas, spirits, and even crawling insects—he perceives and knows entirely their bodily actions, verbal speech, and mental thoughts.

He fully knows all those who possess lust and those who are free from lust; those who possess anger and those who are free from anger; those who possess delusion and those who are free from delusion; those who possess craving and those who are free from craving; those who possess great resolve and conduct and those who do not; those who possess internal and external practice and those who do not; those who possess mindfulness of the wholesome and those who do not; those who possess one-pointed concentration and those who do not; and those who possess a mind of liberation and those who do not. He knows them all completely.
“The Bodhisattva contemplates the five realms— devas, humans, hells, animals, and hungry ghosts—
and clearly distinguishes the names and surnames of his parents, brothers, wives, and children from previous lives,
as well as those of his kin, one by one; he discerns the affairs of one life, ten lives, and hundreds of thousands of billions of countless lifetimes, up to the beginning of heaven and earth.”
During the period when the kalpa has collapsed and become a desolate void, when a single kalpa first begins to form and human beings first emerge,

one is able to know the internal and external names, clothing, food, suffering and joy, the length of lifespans, deaths and births here and there, and the successive destinations of beings throughout ten kalpas, a hundred kalpas, up to countless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas, tracing them from the beginning.
From the very beginning of the head, through all successive bodies—birth, growth, aging, and death; their forms, whether beautiful or ugly;
their states of worthiness or folly, and suffering or joy—he discerns and knows all within the three realms.

He saw that the spirits of people each follow their own karma as they are reborn within the five destinies: some fall into hell, some fall among the animals, some become ghosts or spirits, some are born in the heavens, and some enter human form; among those born in human form, some are born into families of noble rank, wealth, and pleasure, while others are born into families of low status, poverty, and meanness.

He knows that sentient beings are obscured by the five aggregates: first, form; second, sensation; third, perception; fourth, mental formations; and fifth, consciousness. All practice the five desires: the eye craves forms, the ear craves sounds, the nose craves fragrances, the tongue craves flavors, and the body craves tactile sensations. Bound by craving and desire, they may long for peace and happiness through wealth and beauty; from this arise the roots of all evils, and from evil comes suffering.

One who can sever the habitual tendencies of craving and does not follow a lustful mind—even one as minute as a hair—and who practices the Eightfold Path, shall extinguish all suffering; just as there is no fire when there is no fuel, this is called the unconditioned path that transcends the world.

"The Bodhisattva knows for himself that he has already abandoned the root of evil; free from lust, anger, and delusion, he has completely severed the various elements of birth and death and the five aggregates, leaving no further afflictions; what was to be done is accomplished, and his wisdom is fully realized."

When the morning star appeared, he attained great enlightenment, realizing the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and becoming a Most Perfectly Awakened One; he attained the eighteen dharmas of a Buddha, possessing the ten supernatural powers and the four fearlessnesses.
The eighteen qualities of a Buddha refer to the period from his attainment of Buddhahood until his parinirvāṇa:
first, no failure in the Path; second, no empty speech; third, no false intentions; fourth, no impure mind;
fifth, no manifold perceptions; sixth, no lack of mindfulness; seventh, no decline in aspiration.
8. No diminution in vigor; 9. no diminution in concentration of mind;
10. no diminution in wisdom; 11. no diminution in liberation; 12. no diminution in the vision and knowledge of liberation;
13. complete knowledge and vision of past lives; 14. complete knowledge and vision of future lives.
15. He fully knows and sees all matters of the present life; 16. He transforms by assuming various bodily actions based on what he originally knew;
17. He transforms by assuming various verbal actions based on what he originally knew; 18.
He transforms by assuming various mental actions based on what he originally knew—these are the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

Regarding the ten powers: First, the Buddhas perceive and know all things—whether profound, subtle, hidden, or remote; whether they are possible or impossible; and they discern them with clarity as they truly are. This is the first power.
Second, the Buddhas clearly and fully know the stages of conduct performed in the past, present, and future, as well as the places where their retributions will be received. This is the second power.
The Buddha discerns the various distinct thoughts of devas, humans, and sentient beings; this is the third power.
The Buddha knows the many kinds of languages of sentient beings as well as the language of transcending the world; this is the fourth power.
The Buddha fully understands the diverse and immeasurable dispositions of the world; this is the fifth power.
The Buddha is able to manifest the practices of dhyāna, liberation, and samādhi, eliminating the toil and strife of the multitudes; this is the sixth power.
The Buddha knows the bonds of desire and knows the essential requirements for their liberation through appropriate practice; this is the seventh power.
The Buddha’s wisdom is like the ocean, his skillful words are immeasurable, and he recollects all past lives and their experiences; this is the eighth power.

With the pure divine eye, the Buddha perceives the death and rebirth of sentient beings, their good and evil deeds, calamities and blessings, and how they receive retribution according to their actions; this is the ninth power.

The Buddha’s outflows are exhausted, and he is no longer bound by attachments; with his spiritual, true, and sagely wisdom, he has personally realized and witnessed the truth, thoroughly mastered the practice of the Way, accomplished all that can be accomplished, and has no further cycle of birth and death. His wisdom is clear and discerning—this constitutes the tenth supernatural power of a Buddha.
Regarding the "four fearlessnesses": the Buddha possesses divine wisdom and perfect enlightenment; there is nothing he does not know.

Should a fool say, "The Buddha has not fully realized all things," even among the Brahmās and the assembly of sages, none would be able to challenge the Buddha’s wisdom. Thus, he walks alone without apprehension, possessing his first fearlessness.
The Buddha has completely ceased all outflows (*āsrava*), yet ignorant and deluded people say, "The Buddha's outflows are not yet exhausted.
Even among the assembly of noble ones up to the Brahma realm, none can debate the Buddha’s resolve; thus he walks alone without fear—this is the second fearlessness.
The Buddha taught the sutras and precepts, which all under heaven recite and study; yet the foolish and deluded say among themselves, "The Buddha’s sutras can be suppressed.

However, even when reaching the assembly of holy ones such as Brahmā, none are able to debate or disparage the Buddha’s true scriptures. Thus, he walks alone without fear—this is the third fearlessness.
The Buddha manifests the meaning of the Path; his words are true and essential, capable of delivering one from suffering and calamity. Yet those who are ignorant and deluded say:
"He cannot deliver one from suffering.
Even among the assembly of holy ones up to the Brahma realm, none can debate the Buddha’s Right Path. Thus, he travels everywhere without fear—this is the fourfold fearlessness.
The Buddha attained this mind, possessing all-knowing vision; sitting in contemplation, he thought to himself:

"This is truly subtle and wondrous, difficult to know and difficult to clarify, and exceedingly hard to attain. It is lofty and unsurpassed, vast and infinite; it is profound and bottomless, deep and unfathomable. It encompasses heaven and earth in its greatness and penetrates the infinitesimal gaps of existence. It nurtures and sustains all sentient beings as if looking upon an only child. Having served successive Buddhas and accumulated immeasurable merit, enduring diligent toil through kalpas without forgetting his past efforts, he has now fully realized it all."
He spoke this verse in praise:
"The reward for performing merit is blissful; all manifold aspirations shall be fulfilled.
One swiftly enters profound stillness and attains nirvāṇa."
"Now I have realized that the Buddha is most noble; having abandoned lust, he is pure and without outflows.
He is able to lead all beings, and those who follow him will surely be joyful.

At that time, the Buddha was at the site of the Excellent Enlightenment (Sudharmā-maṇḍala) beneath the Peepal tree in the realm of Magadha; by the power of his virtue he had subdued Māra, his enlightened wisdom was divinely tranquil, and his threefold knowledge was unimpeded.
He delivered the two merchants, Trapusa and Bhallika, by granting them the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, thereby establishing them as lay disciples (*upāsaka*).
He then recalled how Dīpaṃkara Buddha had distinguished him as a future Buddha, saying:

"A hundred kalpas hence, you shall attain Buddhahood, named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān; you shall deliver and liberate sentient beings just as I do now."

"From that time forth, I have established great vows and practiced the six perfections, the four immeasurables, the four debts of gratitude, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. Adapting skillful means to the times, I have accumulated all dharmas without weariness; my lofty conduct was extraordinary, I endured immeasurable suffering, and I never neglected the fruits of my merit, so that my great vow has now been fulfilled."
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the entire assembly was filled with great joy; they paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
*The Sutra on the Original Acts of the Practice*, Scroll Lower.
